reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: Pincer nail is characterised by excessive transverse over-curvature of the plate that increases from proximal to distal, pinching the underlying soft tissue
The tightening curve traps and compresses the nail bed and distal tissue, which is the source of the often severe pain
The great toenail is most commonly involved, and the deformity may be hereditary or acquired
Acquired forms are associated with degenerative bony changes of the underlying phalanx, ill-fitting footwear, osteoarthritis, and some medications
A dorsal bony spur or widening of the distal phalanx often underlies acquired cases and is best shown on radiograph
As the curve deepens the lateral edges may roll inward, sometimes producing subungual hyperkeratosis and secondary changes
Management ranges from conservative measures such as bracing and orthonyxia to surgical correction of the matrix or underlying bone in refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Pincer nail results from progressive transverse over-curvature of the nail plate, so that the two lateral edges curl toward each other and increasingly compress the nail bed and pulp as the nail grows distally. In many acquired cases an underlying bony change of the distal phalanx, such as a dorsal osteophyte or lateral widening, alters the shape of the tissue on which the matrix sits and forces the plate to curl. Hereditary forms reflect an intrinsic tendency of the matrix to produce an over-curved plate. The pinching action distorts and can even resorb the underlying soft tissue and bone, and the trapped nail bed generates pain and predisposes to secondary ingrowing and hyperkeratosis.
additionalDifferentials: Psoriatic or degenerative nail bed disease
Congenital malalignment of the great toenail
additionalInvestigations: Radiograph of the distal phalanx to identify a dorsal spur or bony widening
Clinical measurement of the degree of transverse curvature along the nail
Assessment of footwear and biomechanical factors
Examination for coexisting osteoarthritis or systemic disease
Review of medications associated with acquired over-curvature
Onychoscopy to assess nail bed and lateral fold involvement
redFlags: Severe unremitting pain interfering with walking and function
Secondary infection or ulceration of the pinched soft tissue
Radiographic bony resorption or an aggressive-looking underlying lesion
Rapidly progressive deformity or an atypical single-nail change suggesting a tumour
reference.prognosis: Conservative bracing can relieve symptoms and partially flatten the curve but tends to relapse when discontinued, whereas surgery addressing the matrix or underlying bony spur offers the most durable correction in refractory, painful cases.
pitfalls: Treating the nail as a simple ingrowing toenail and missing the underlying over-curvature
Omitting a radiograph and overlooking a correctable bony spur
Expecting conservative bracing alone to cure severe long-standing deformity
Failing to address footwear and biomechanical contributors, leading to recurrence
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
management: Offer conservative bracing (orthonyxia) to gradually flatten the transverse over-curvature and relieve pain, accepting a tendency to relapse when discontinued
Modify footwear to remove external pressure and address biomechanical contributors
Treat associated pain and secondary ingrowing with analgesia and care of the compressed nail bed
Manage recalcitrant lateral in-rolling with partial nail avulsion and matricectomy, using phenolisation of the lateral matrix horns
Undertake durable surgical correction of the underlying dorsal bony spur or phalangeal widening, with matrix or nail-bed reconstruction, in refractory painful cases
Treat coexisting subungual hyperkeratosis and review medications and osteoarthritis associated with acquired over-curvature
